scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In 1826, Sir Henry Rowley Bishop set lyrics by General John Burgoyne to music, creating a tune so infectious it became the regimental march of the Royal Berkshire Regiment and a staple at West Point.
This is Dashing White Sergeant. 19th century.

Title card: Dashing White Sergeant · Scotland · 19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The title originates from 18th-century lyrics by General John Burgoyne, set to music in 1826 by English composer Sir Henry Rowley Bishop.
Though intended for an opera, it became a military march for the Royal Berkshire Regiment and a staple at West Point Military Academy.
The dance steps themselves are derived from Swedish circle dancing, which was a popular trend in Victorian-era Britain.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: As a progressive social dance, it is designed to facilitate meeting multiple partners.
It is a standard feature at Scottish weddings, ceilidhs, and formal balls, as well as military functions where the tune serves as a march.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form a circle of six, usually three men and three women alternating.
They circle anti-clockwise for eight counts, then clockwise for eight.
The circle splits into two sets of three.
Watch for The Arch, The Stamp and Clap.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (Wm_5l_bs-6Y)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Starts as a circle of six, transitions to two lines of three facing each other, moves linearly through the room.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to a reel in 4/4 time.
Key musical versions include the original 1826 Bishop composition and a later arrangement by Sir Hugh S. Roberton for the Glasgow Orpheus Choir.
Listen for the Fiddle, Accordion, Piano, Drums.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 110 beats a minute.
A bright, driving 4/4 reel with a military march undertone. The melody is characterized by ascending leaps and a steady, percussive pulse suitable for marching or dancing.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Usually performed in social halls or ballrooms with wooden floors.
Dancers often wear traditional Scottish dress, such as kilts for men and white dresses with tartan sashes for women, though it is also performed in casual attire at modern ceilidhs.

narration: Sir Henry Rowley Bishop (composer), General John Burgoyne (lyricist), and Sir Hugh S. Roberton (choral arranger).
